domain.title: Systems and delivery
domain.summary: How software runs and ships: processes, networks, configuration, containers, pipelines, caches, concurrency, and distributed failure.

concepts.title: Networking basics
concepts.summary: DNS, TCP connections, TLS, and latency — the substrate every remote call depends on.
learningObjectives: Trace what happens between resolving a hostname and receiving the first response byte
Explain why network calls are slower and less reliable than function calls
Identify connection reuse and pooling in client code
recognitionSignals: HTTP agent, keep-alive, or connection reuse options on outbound clients
TLS or certificate settings such as rejectUnauthorized, NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED, or custom CA bundles
host resolution details such as localhost vs service hostnames or IPv4/IPv6 selection
server listen address and port choices such as 0.0.0.0 vs 127.0.0.1
misconceptionPatterns: Treating a remote call like a local function call
Assuming the network is reliable and latency is zero
Disabling certificate verification to fix a TLS error

concepts.title: Configuration
concepts.summary: Separating environment-specific settings from code, and validating them before the application relies on them.
learningObjectives: Explain why configuration should differ by environment while code stays the same
Identify configuration read lazily in a way that fails late in production
Design fail-fast validation for required settings
recognitionSignals: environment variable reads (process.env, os.environ, os.Getenv)
.env files or config modules
feature flags
defaults applied when a variable is missing
misconceptionPatterns: Silently defaulting a required production setting
Assuming build-time and runtime environment variables behave the same
Scattering environment reads throughout the codebase

concepts.title: Concurrency
concepts.summary: Making progress on several tasks over overlapping time periods, and the ordering and shared-state hazards that creates.

related.boundary: Races on database rows map there; races on in-process state map here.

learningObjectives: Explain how Promise.all changes execution, latency, and error behavior compared to sequential awaits
Identify race conditions in interleaved async operations
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism
recognitionSignals: concurrent fan-out such as Promise.all/allSettled, asyncio.gather, or goroutines with WaitGroup/errgroup
multiple requests started before any of them is awaited
shared in-memory variables updated from concurrent async callbacks
check-then-act on in-process state with an await in between (database read-then-write maps to db.isolation-levels)
misconceptionPatterns: Believing Promise.all cancels remaining work when one promise rejects
Assuming single-threaded runtimes have no race conditions across awaits
Believing a promise's work starts only when it is awaited, so creating several promises before awaiting them runs them one at a time

concepts.title: Processes and threads
concepts.summary: Operating-system units of execution: isolated processes, shared-memory threads, and how runtimes like Node map work onto them.
learningObjectives: Explain how the event loop, worker threads, and separate processes differ
Predict what blocks the event loop and its effect on all requests
Choose between threads, processes, and separate services for CPU-heavy work
recognitionSignals: worker threads, subprocesses, or process pools (worker_threads, child_process, multiprocessing)
CPU-heavy synchronous work on a request path (large JSON parsing, hashing, image processing, regex on large input)
synchronous file-system or crypto APIs (readFileSync, pbkdf2Sync) inside request handlers
offloading CPU-bound work to a separate service or background job
misconceptionPatterns: Believing async makes CPU-bound work non-blocking
Believing worker threads or subprocesses share ordinary in-memory variables with the main thread
Believing one slow synchronous request only delays itself, rather than every request on that instance

concepts.title: Bounded concurrency
concepts.summary: Limiting how much work runs at once so a burst of tasks cannot overwhelm memory, connections, or downstream services.
learningObjectives: Explain under what workload unbounded Promise.all becomes dangerous
Implement or evaluate a concurrency limit using a pool or semaphore
Choose a limit based on downstream capacity and rate limits
recognitionSignals: Promise.all or equivalent fan-out over a user- or data-sized array
concurrency limiters such as p-limit, p-map's concurrency option, semaphores, or worker pools
concurrency settings on job-queue workers or consumers
splitting a large collection into fixed-size chunks specifically to cap in-flight work
misconceptionPatterns: Believing more concurrency always means more throughput
Ignoring downstream rate limits and pool sizes
Assuming arrays passed to Promise.all stay small

concepts.title: Backpressure
concepts.summary: Signaling producers to slow down when consumers cannot keep up, instead of buffering until something falls over.
learningObjectives: Identify where unbounded buffering occurs between a producer and consumer
Compare dropping, blocking, and rejecting as responses to overload
Design backpressure for a streaming or queue-based pipeline
recognitionSignals: stream write() calls or ReadableStream controllers that ignore the drain event, write() return value, or desiredSize
in-memory arrays or queues that incoming requests or events push onto without a size limit
servers rejecting or shedding work (e.g. 429/503) when an internal queue or buffer is full
highWaterMark, max queue length, queue depth, or consumer lag settings and metrics
misconceptionPatterns: Believing a bigger buffer or queue fixes sustained overload rather than delaying the failure
Believing a concurrency limiter bounds memory, when tasks waiting for a slot accumulate in an unbounded pending queue
Assuming a stream write is flushed immediately, so its return value can be ignored

concepts.title: Caching
concepts.summary: Keeping computed or fetched results closer to where they are needed, and deciding when they stop being true.
learningObjectives: Explain cache hit, miss, TTL, and invalidation for a specific cache
Identify data that must never be cached across users
Compare caching layers such as HTTP, CDN, framework, and application memory
recognitionSignals: Cache-Control, Vary, or ETag headers
framework data-cache APIs such as Next.js "use cache", cacheTag/revalidateTag, revalidate, or fetch cache options
module-scope maps or LRU structures used as memoization caches
Redis or key-value store reads before database queries, with TTLs or explicit invalidation
misconceptionPatterns: Caching personalized responses under a shared key
Believing in-process caches are shared across instances
Adding a cache without an invalidation strategy

concepts.title: Containers
concepts.summary: Packaging an application with its runtime dependencies into an image that runs the same way across environments.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between an image and a running container
Evaluate a Dockerfile for layer caching, image size, and secret exposure
Identify why a container behaves differently from the developer's machine
recognitionSignals: container build or compose files (Dockerfile, Containerfile, compose.yaml)
multi-stage builds
container environment variables and exposed ports
health checks
misconceptionPatterns: Believing containers provide strong security isolation by default, when they share the host kernel
Believing a secret passed via ARG/ENV or deleted in a later RUN step is gone from the final image
Assuming running as root inside a container is harmless because the container is isolated
Assuming the app will stop cleanly on SIGTERM when it runs as PID 1 behind a shell-form CMD or without its own signal handler

concepts.title: CI/CD pipelines
concepts.summary: Automating build, test, and deploy steps so every change reaches production through the same verified path.
learningObjectives: Trace what a pipeline runs for a pull request versus a merge to main
Identify pipeline steps that expose secrets to untrusted code
Design a deploy sequence that supports rollback
recognitionSignals: CI configuration files (.github/workflows, .gitlab-ci.yml, CircleCI config)
build, test, and deploy job definitions
secrets referenced in pipeline configuration
pull_request_target or workflow triggers
misconceptionPatterns: Believing fork pull requests can never reach repository secrets, when pull_request_target and workflow_run run in the base repository's context with secrets and its GITHUB_TOKEN
Believing a green pipeline means the deploy is safe
Believing a version tag such as @v4 on a third-party action is immutable, so pinning to a full commit SHA is unnecessary

concepts.title: Distributed failure
concepts.summary: In systems spanning multiple processes and machines, partial failure, duplication, and ambiguous outcomes are normal, not exceptional.

related.boundary: Atomic writes within a single database map there.

learningObjectives: Explain why a remote call can have three outcomes: success, failure, or unknown
Analyze a workflow spanning a database and an external service for inconsistency windows
Defend a design such as an outbox, saga, or reconciliation job for a specific failure mode
recognitionSignals: a database write and an external API call or event publish in the same code path
external calls or message publishes made inside a database transaction
outbox tables, saga steps, or compensating actions
reconciliation or sync jobs comparing local state with a third party
misconceptionPatterns: Believing a database transaction also makes an API call or message publish made inside it atomic with the write
Assuming events and webhooks arrive in the order they were produced
Believing a committed local write will reach downstream services without a durable handoff such as an outbox or reconciliation

concepts.title: Instances and runtime lifecycle
concepts.summary: Production code runs in many replaceable instances — long-running servers, serverless functions, or containers — that start cold, get frozen or terminated, and share nothing in memory.

related.boundary: Connection counts per instance and pooler behavior map there.

learningObjectives: Predict whether work started after a response is returned will complete on a serverless versus a long-running runtime
Identify module-level or in-memory state that breaks when requests are served by different instances
Design graceful shutdown that stops accepting work and drains in-flight requests on a termination signal
recognitionSignals: un-awaited promises or background work after returning a response, or waitUntil/after() style APIs
module-scope variables used as counters, rate limiters, sessions, or caches
expensive initialization at module scope reused across warm invocations (SDK clients, config loading)
SIGTERM/SIGINT handlers, server.close, or shutdown hooks
runtime or deployment settings such as edge vs Node runtime, max function duration, or instance counts
misconceptionPatterns: Believing a serverless function keeps running un-awaited work after the response has been returned
Assuming module-level state persists and is shared across all requests in production
Assuming a process gets unlimited time to finish work after receiving SIGTERM
